title: Predictive audio representations for early detection and tracking of hidden dynamic objects

paper.title: Predictive audio representations for early detection and tracking of hidden dynamic objects
paper.abstract: Abstract Predicting potential dangers is core to safety. Forecasting the presence of other traffic agents is core to danger prediction. Occluded traffic agents challenge detection systems as they might become visible too late, leaving the autonomous vehicle too little time to identify, plan and act accordingly in a robust and safe way. Previous works proved that auditory perception, being omnidirectional and not constrained by a field-of-view , provides fundamental cues for early spotting of different road users, even when hidden by other vehicles or infrastructures. Yet, those contributions deal with scenarios with only one vehicle present, and they either identify the type of vehicle or estimate its direction of arrival. In this work, we move forward, and propose a multi-task system which, simultaneously, estimates the number of vehicles present, their type, and their direction of arrival. Our methodological contribution is a two-stage pipeline: a self-supervised pre-training stage inspired by the Joint- Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) applied directly to multichannel raw waveforms, followed by supervised multi-task fine-tuning with a bidirectional LSTM and three classification heads. The pre-training stage trains the encoder without labels, pushing it to predict the latent representation of a future audio segment from its past context. To train and test our framework, since no suitable dataset was publicly available, we collected an ad-hoc one covering Non-Line-Of-Sight scenarios with multiple traffic agents simultaneously operating. Experimental evaluation shows that our method outperforms the state of the art; it also proves that our design choice allows the model to learn robust representations, which can be transferred to an unseen driving scenario, maintaining reasonable and stable performance.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Safe navigation requires anticipating road users that are not yet visible. Cameras and LiDARs can only operate when there is line of sight. Although the same does not apply to automotive radars, able to penetrate non-conductive materials like plastic bumpers and glass, they still cannot see through the metallic bodies of potential in-between vehicles, resulting in a limited field of view . Sound propagates, and encodes spatial information, easily around obstacles, making acoustic perception extremely valuable in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios, such as vehicles approaching a T-junction from a hidden street. Prior investigations demonstrated that a microphone array can estimate the presence of an approaching vehicle before it becomes visible [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . These results are encouraging: yet, these works address scenarios where a single vehicle is present, and while they recover the direction of arrival, they do not identify the type of vehicle. A system operating in the real world, though, interacts with multiple simultaneous traffic agents: to do so safely and robustly, it needs to know the location and also the nature of those agents. Different types of vehicles, indeed, have different performance characteristics, kinematics, and movement limits ( e.g. , a city bus has a much wider turning radius and slower manoeuvrability than a car), which strongly condition planning and risk assessment. Acoustic traffic monitoring systems [ 5 ] provide those estimates, but operate at minute-level granularity on fixed roadside infrastructure, thus they are not directly usable by an autonomous vehicle. Fig. 1 : Example of a typical use-case: a car is approaching from the left and a van is approaching from the right at T-junction with buildings occluding them. The 8-microphone on-board array captures their raw audio signatures, which a self-supervised pretrained encoder maps into latent embeddings. A supervised head then aggregates a 3-second window of these embeddings to predict, at every second, the direction, number, and type of the non-line-of-sight vehicles. This letter addresses this gap. We present a multi-task acoustic perception framework that simultaneously classifies, at one-second resolution, the direction of arrival (DoA) of sound sources outside the field-of-view ( e.g. , left, right), and predicts the number of vehicles in the scene, together with their class, by using only the raw waveform from an 8-microphone circular array. A schematic representation of the system is provided in Fig. 1 . While we acknowledge that handling the simultaneous presence of only 2 2 vehicles may appear as a limitation of our approach, the challenges that arise in multi-vehicle scenes are mainly related to the ability to detect and parse the presence of more than one simultaneous spectral signature. Our goal is to provide a proof-of-concept that it is possible to develop a multi-task pipeline able to handle planar localisation, classification and vehicle counting without relying on any sound-source separation method. Sound source separation, indeed, is pretty much still an open problem, especially in the wild [ 6 ] . Such a proof-of-concept can serve as a baseline for further approaches coping with several vehicles. Our methodological contribution is a two-stage pipeline: a self-supervised pre-training stage inspired by the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) [ 7 , 8 ] , applied directly to multichannel raw waveforms without spectral pre-processing, followed by supervised multi-task fine-tuning with a bidirectional LSTM and three classification heads. Rather than reconstructing raw audio, the encoder is trained to predict the latent representation of a future acoustic segment from its past context, thereby adopting a temporal prediction objective that encourages semantically meaningful structure and yields representations that are temporally stable and transferable across driving conditions.

sections.heading: II Related Work
sections.text: Acoustic vehicle perception. Audio has been explored both as a complement to visual sensing and as an independent modality for early detection of traffic agents outside the field of view [ 9 , 10 ] . The first dataset explicitly designed to address NLOS scenarios was introduced in [ 1 ] , where the authors used SRP-PHAT [ 11 ] and a linear SVM to estimate the Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) of a vehicle, expressed as left, front, right, none . Subsequent work improved direction accuracy using CNN architectures [ 2 ] , jointly predicted the approach and departure directions [ 3 ] , and integrated acoustic cues with bird’s-eye-view spatial priors [ 4 ] . All these works perform only DoA estimation in single-vehicle scenarios. The DCASE community, through the Acoustic-Based Traffic Monitoring challenge and its baseline system [ 5 ] , investigated multi-vehicle localisation and classification relying on fixed roadside arrays. Yet, this setting does not fit the requirements of an autonomous vehicle’s planner: the sensors are stationary, rather than on-board, and estimates are provided every minute, making them very valuable for traffic monitoring, but not to trigger immediate interventions. Self-supervised audio representations. Contrastive methods [ 12 ] and masked reconstruction approaches [ 13 , 14 ] have shown that representations learned without labels on a large audio dataset can be reused across a broad range of downstream audio tasks. The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture [ 8 , 15 ] proposes a different objective: a predictor is trained to forecast the latent representation of a masked or future region from context, avoiding the cost of reconstructing perceptually irrelevant signal detail. Audio-JEPA [ 16 ] adapts this principle to mel-spectrogram patches and achieves competitive results on general audio benchmarks with large amounts of training data. We adapt the JEPA temporal prediction paradigm to operate directly on multichannel raw waveforms, letting the encoder free to learn from the raw signal whichever spectral, temporal, and cross-channel structure the prediction task actually rewards. Our contribution can be summarised as follows: 1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first on-board acoustic system that jointly estimates the direction , the number , and the class of multiple NLOS vehicles, with 1 1 -second latency. 2. We introduce a JEPA-inspired temporal-prediction objective trained directly on raw 8-channel waveforms, and show that it captures better representations than supervised models, which allows generalisation to unseen, and significantly different, scenarios.

sections.heading: III Method
sections.text: We divide the description of the proposed framework into three parts: the temporal windowing of the input signal (Section III-A ), the self-supervised pre-training of the acoustic encoder (Section III-B ), and the supervised multi-task fine-tuning stage (Section III-C ). An overview of the full pipeline is shown in Fig. 2 .

Each frame is represented as a raw waveform tensor 𝐱 ∈ ℝ M × L \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times L} , where L = f s = 48 ​ K L=f_{s}=48K samples. Consecutive frames are grouped into sliding windows of length T = 3 T=3 seconds. sections.heading: IV Experiments
sections.text: We run three main experiments: we evaluate the performance of our multi-task model and compare it with the state of the art ( Experiment 1 ); we carry out ablation studies to experimentally evaluate the rationale of our design choices ( Experiment 2 ); we investigate whether the model can generalise and robustly operate on unseen, and significantly different, scenarios ( Experiment 3 ). We indicate the three tasks: DoA estimation, vehicle type classification and number of vehicle estimation as Direction , Count and Type , respectively. Some qualitative results conclude the section.

sections.heading: IV-A The Dataset
sections.text: To collect real‑world data, three MER2‑503‑36U3C cameras were mounted side‑by‑side on the roof of a vehicle, directly above an octagonal array of eight microphones. A GPS unit was also installed on the roof. An overview of the setup is shown in Fig. 3 . Each camera provides a 93 93 ° FoV at a resolution of 2448 × 2048 2448\times 2048 px at 20 20 fps, resulting in a combined horizontal coverage of approximately 279 279 °. Fig. 3 : Sensor configuration used in data collection. In (a): schematic top-view representation; In (b), GPS (1) and camera–microphone (2) system mounted on the vehicle. Data collection took place at the SolarPark in Oldenburg, Germany. The dataset spans across 6 6 different scenarios ( cf. , Fig. 4 ), grouped into two main settings leading to two different datasets: the one we refer to as the T-Junction (TJ) one and the Take-Over (TO) one. In both cases, trials last between 10 10 and 30 30 s, depending on the vehicle’s speed and position. To reduce bias toward specific engine signatures, two different cars and two different vans were used. In the T-junction (TJ) dataset, the ego-vehicle is stationary at a T-junction. The dataset contains 6,827 6{,}827 labeled audio frames of 1 1 s: 1,958 1{,}958 with no vehicle present, 2,264 2{,}264 with a single vehicle approaching (left-to-right or right-to-left), and 2,605 2{,}605 with two vehicles approaching. In the Take Over (TO) dataset, the ego-vehicle is in motion, and one or two vehicles perform an overtake manoeuvre. The dataset contains 3,005 3{,}005 one-second labeled audio frames: 2,263 2{,}263 with one vehicle, and 742 742 with two. To annotate the dataset, when labels are not available directly from the experiments’ design, we leveraged the cameras and the labels given by YOLOv26x [ 19 ] running on the front camera images for static scenarios and on all three camera images for the others (mistakes were manually corrected). We assign labels for all the tasks we carry on: three classes ( 0 0 , 1 1 , 2 2 ) to indicate the numer of vehicles in the scene; four classes ( car, van, car+van, none ) to indicate the vehicle type, and five classes ( left, front, right, none, both ) to represent the direction of arrival/departure of a vehicle. More specifically, we assign the front label to any vehicle visible in the front camera’s 93 ∘ 93^{\circ} cone, left to vehicles entering or leaving via the left camera, and right via the right camera. The label both refers to two vehicles approaching from opposite directions, the label none indicates no vehicles. In the driving scenarios, a vehicle that has not yet reached either lateral camera is labelled as back . (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) (f) Fig. 4 : Reference scenarios ; ego-vehicle in blue. (a-d) static (T-junction): one (a) or two vehicles (b,c) approaching from the same direction (one vehicle occluding the other); two vehicles approaching from different directions (d). (e-f) driving (take-over): one (e) or two vehicles (f) approaching from the back and overtaking the ego-vehicle. All models are trained and evaluated on the TJ dataset: 5,458 5{,}458 frames for training, 1,369 1{,}369 frames across 78 78 for validation. The TO dataset is held out from all training stages, including self-supervised pre-training, and is used only for the cross-scenario evaluation of Section IV-D .

sections.heading: IV-B Experiment 1
sections.text: Table I shows the performance of our model (indicated as Proposed ), and a comparison against the state of the art. We evaluate the accuracy in the Direction tasks of the models in [ 1 ] , [ 3 ] , and [ 2 ] , trained and tested on the TJ dataset (same split). Those models rely on a four-class schema for single-vehicle scenarios. Our method uses the extended five-class taxonomy, covering multiple simultaneous vehicles. Compared to the strongest prior result, even considering an additional class, our approach yields a 9.1 % 9.1\% improvement. We believe this is due to the JEPA-inspired stage of our method, capturing better representations compared to SOTA supervised models, and perform well also on smaller datasets, like ours. As being the only other work carrying out all three tasks, we also compare ourselves against [ 5 ] , trained and tested on the TJ dataset (same split). Our model shows an improvement of 21.2 % 21.2\% in the Direction task, 40.1 % 40.1\% in the Type task, and 5.6 % 5.6\% in the Count task. Table II (left columns) reports per-class recall on the TJ validation set. Classes none ( 94.4 % 94.4\% ) and both ( 100.0 % 100.0\% ) are the ones characterised by the highest accuracy: the absence of any acoustic source and the simultaneous presence of two vehicles coming from both sides produce discriminating signatures. The most often confused is the front class ( 60.0 % 60.0\% ), with the BiLSTM reacting with some delay to the class change. For instance, a vehicle approaching from the left, whose DoA is initially, and correctly, classified as left might be kept considered as such when it enters the front class. More details are provided in Section IV-E2 . Recall in the Count task exceeds 93 % 93\% across all classes, indicating that the self-supervised learning (SSL) representations encode the presence and number of distinct acoustic sources, without any architecture designed for counting. Vans achieve the highest recall ( 97.0 % 97.0\% ) in the Type task, likely due to their distinctive low-frequency engine signature.

sections.heading: IV-C Experiment 2
sections.text: Table I includes also the results of ablation studies run to experimentally evaluate the rationale of our design choices. We can observe that the LSTM-only baseline provides the worst performance: without the SSL inductive bias, the supervised signal alone is insufficient to learn generalised representations. We also note that the difference between frozen and unfrozen learning at stage 2 does not impact performance much, but helps better appreciate the direction task. The Ablation - prediction-target compares three configurations of the same encoder-predictor architecture, differing only in which frames act as context and target. The two-step horizon predicts 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} from 𝐱 n − 2 \mathbf{x}_{n-2} ; the one-step variant predicts 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} from 𝐱 n − 1 \mathbf{x}_{n-1} ; the interpolation variant recovers 𝐱 n − 1 \mathbf{x}_{n-1} from { 𝐱 n − 2 , 𝐱 n } \{\mathbf{x}_{n-2},\mathbf{x}_{n}\} . In the Ablation - context window , the two-step horizon yields the best performance ( 81.8 % 81.8\% direction, vs. 80.8 % 80.8\% one-step and 79.3 % 79.3\% interpolation), and is our default. One possible interpretation is that one-step prediction can be largely achieved by extending short-time spectral content from the immediately preceding frame, providing a weaker inductive bias than the longer horizon; conversely, predicting the masked intermediate frame from a bidirectional context turns the pretext task closer to reconstruction than to forecasting. sections.heading: IV-D Experiment 3
sections.text: We investigate whether the model can generalise to unseen scenarios. The TO dataset is held out from all training stages. After training on the static TJ dataset, we compare three adaptation strategies: • Option A ( head-only ): the SSL encoder f θ f_{\theta} is frozen; only the BiLSTM, shared MLP, and heads are fine-tuned. • Option B ( full-model ): all components are fine-tuned, with a small encoder learning rate ( η enc = 10 − 5 \eta_{\mathrm{enc}}{=}10^{-5} ) to limit forgetting. • Option C ( SSL re-pretraining + head ): the temporal-prediction objective (Section III-B ) is re-applied for 30 30 epochs on the unlabeled support audio, updating the encoder only; the BiLSTM and heads are then fine-tuned as in Option A. The TO dataset introduces one new direction class, back , absent from the static training set. The direction head is extended from 5 5 to 6 6 output neurons before fine-tuning, with the back weights and bias initialised to zero; the count and type heads are unchanged. One shot is one complete take-over data point ( 10 10 - 30 30 one-second frames). Each ( K ​ -shot , Option ) (K\text{-shot},\text{Option}) configuration is evaluated over N = 10 N{=}10 random draws; fine-tuning runs for 15 15 epochs at η head = 5 × 10 − 4 \eta_{\mathrm{head}}{=}5{\times}10^{-4} , with the same weighting λ = 5 \lambda{=}5 as in base training. Direction recall is computed only over classes present in the TO data; none and both are excluded.

sections.heading: IV-D 1 Zero-shot transfer
sections.text: At K = 0 K{=}0 , overall direction accuracy is 2.3 % 2.3\% , effectively zero by construction: the back neuron is initialised to zero and cannot be predicted until the head receives gradient updates. Count and type accuracy collapse to 8.2 % 8.2\% and 6.5 % 6.5\% , reflecting the distribution shift between stationary and dynamic conditions.

sections.heading: IV-D 2 Few-shot adaptation
sections.text: With K = 5 K{=}5 support points, overall direction accuracy reaches 54.5 54.5 - 55.8 % 55.8\% across the three options, rising to 69.2 69.2 - 70.1 % 70.1\% at K = 10 K{=}10 (Table II ). The ranking among options is not stable across shot counts, and the spread between them is small relative to the standard deviation across the N = 10 N{=}10 random data points. We read this as evidence that the three strategies are practically equivalent at the support sizes tested: the frozen SSL representations already suffice for driving-scenario adaptation, and neither full-model fine-tuning (Option B) nor SSL re-pretraining (Option C) measurably beats head-only adaptation (Option A). The same near-equivalence holds for count and type.

sections.heading: IV-E 1 Detection horizon outside the Field-of-View (FoV)
sections.text: For each of the 38 38 validation scenarios where vehicles are entering the FoV approaching it from the left/right, the detection horizon is defined as the longest run of consecutive 1 1 s frames classified correctly, ending at the frame immediately preceding the vehicle’s entry into the camera’s FoV. A single frame classified differently terminates the run, so the metric is conservative. The model achieves a mean detection horizon of 4.6 4.6 s (median 5.0 5.0 s), with 77 % 77\% of scenarios providing at least 1 1 s of advance prediction and 62 % 62\% at least 3 3 s. Those results further highlight the benefits in the use of sound to anticipate the presence of a traffic agent before it becomes visible, allowing for longer response times and increased safety. sections.heading: IV-E 2 Front-class error pathology
sections.text: In Experiment 1 the front class yield 60.0 % 60.0\% recall. In an attempt to investigate the reasons making it the hardest to recognise, we analyse when most errors take place. The intuition is that the Direction classes, identified by the cone described in Figure 3 are rather arbitrary and not acoustically grounded, thus mistakes in the transitions are physiological . We divide the class into three subclasses: entering, front, leaving . The entering subclass contains all samples corresponding to the first 1 1 s frame where the vehicle just becomes visible when entering the “front visible cone” from left or right. The leaving subclass contains all samples corresponding to the last 1 1 s frame where the vehicle is still visible before leaving from the “front visible cone” heading left or right. The front subclass contains all the remaining samples from the original front class. Fig. 5 reports the results of the analysis. As we can see, most mistakes happen when “transitioning” from the left / right classes to the front and viceversa, supporting the initial intuition.

sections.heading: IV-E 3 Dynamics and Types Representations
sections.text: We analyse the SSL latent abilities to capture jointly the dynamics and the type of the sound sources, and ask what the representation actually contains without supervision. Figure 6 shows a UMAP [ 20 ] projection of the learned latents. Three structural facts are visible. First, silence consistently lives outside the active manifold: the none class of direction, the 0 class of count, and the none class of type occupy the same peripheral islands, indicating a stable no vehicle state separated from any vehicle activity. Second, the dominant axis within the active manifold separates one-vehicle from two-vehicle scenarios. Figure 6 -b shows a clean spatial gradient with two-vehicle frames ( 2 ) on the left and one-vehicle frames ( 1 ) on the right. Figure 6 -c inherits this structure since two-vehicle scenarios are always car+van pairs by recording protocol. Third, within the one-vehicle subset of 6 -c, car is less clustered than van , demonstrating a weaker representation of this class. Figure 6 -a shows that direction-of-arrival classes form recognisable regions: left (blue) and right (green) occupy opposite sides of the active manifold, both (orange) clusters tightly on the left edge where the two-vehicle region lies, and front (yellow) intermixes with the others, partially in coherence with the two opposite sides, but also highlighting the encoder’s limits to capture the spatial structure of that class. sections.heading: V CONCLUSION
sections.text: We introduced a multi-task acoustic perception framework that estimates the direction, the number, and the type of occluded vehicles in the scene. The framework works directly on the raw audio signals and provides robust predictions every second. Experimental evaluation showed that our method outperforms the state of the art, and further stressed the crucial role that auditory perception can play. Future work might proceed along two main directions: the extension to scenarios with more than 2 vehicles present, where localisation is refined to a regression task ( i.e. , from classes to continuous angles), and the integration into a multimodal system.

Forecasting the presence of other traffic agents is core to danger prediction. Occluded traffic agents challenge detection systems as they might become visible too late, leaving the autonomous vehicle too little time to identify, plan and act accordingly in a robust and safe way. Previous works proved that auditory perception, being omnidirectional and not constrained by a field-of-view , provides fundamental cues for early spotting of different road users, even when hidden by other vehicles or infrastructures. Yet, those contributions deal with scenarios with only one vehicle present, and they either identify the type of vehicle or estimate its direction of arrival. In this work, we move forward, and propose a multi-task system which, simultaneously, estimates the number of vehicles present, their type, and their direction of arrival. Our methodological contribution is a two-stage pipeline: a self-supervised pre-training stage inspired by the Joint- Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) applied directly to multichannel raw waveforms, followed by supervised multi-task fine-tuning with a bidirectional LSTM and three classification heads. The pre-training stage trains the encoder without labels, pushing it to predict the latent representation of a future audio segment from its past context. To train and test our framework, since no suitable dataset was publicly available, we collected an ad-hoc one covering Non-Line-Of-Sight scenarios with multiple traffic agents simultaneously operating. Experimental evaluation shows that our method outperforms the state of the art; it also proves that our design choice allows the model to learn robust representations, which can be transferred to an unseen driving scenario, maintaining reasonable and stable performance. Index Terms: Driverless Vehicles, Auditory Perception, Machine Learning, Audio Signal Processing I Introduction Safe navigation requires anticipating road users that are not yet visible. Cameras and LiDARs can only operate when there is line of sight. Although the same does not apply to automotive radars, able to penetrate non-conductive materials like plastic bumpers and glass, they still cannot see through the metallic bodies of potential in-between vehicles, resulting in a limited field of view . Sound propagates, and encodes spatial information, easily around obstacles, making acoustic perception extremely valuable in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios, such as vehicles approaching a T-junction from a hidden street. Prior investigations demonstrated that a microphone array can estimate the presence of an approaching vehicle before it becomes visible [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . These results are encouraging: yet, these works address scenarios where a single vehicle is present, and while they recover the direction of arrival, they do not identify the type of vehicle. A system operating in the real world, though, interacts with multiple simultaneous traffic agents: to do so safely and robustly, it needs to know the location and also the nature of those agents. Different types of vehicles, indeed, have different performance characteristics, kinematics, and movement limits ( e.g. , a city bus has a much wider turning radius and slower manoeuvrability than a car), which strongly condition planning and risk assessment. Acoustic traffic monitoring systems [ 5 ] provide those estimates, but operate at minute-level granularity on fixed roadside infrastructure, thus they are not directly usable by an autonomous vehicle. Fig. 1 : Example of a typical use-case: a car is approaching from the left and a van is approaching from the right at T-junction with buildings occluding them. The 8-microphone on-board array captures their raw audio signatures, which a self-supervised pretrained encoder maps into latent embeddings. A supervised head then aggregates a 3-second window of these embeddings to predict, at every second, the direction, number, and type of the non-line-of-sight vehicles. This letter addresses this gap. We present a multi-task acoustic perception framework that simultaneously classifies, at one-second resolution, the direction of arrival (DoA) of sound sources outside the field-of-view ( e.g. , left, right), and predicts the number of vehicles in the scene, together with their class, by using only the raw waveform from an 8-microphone circular array. A schematic representation of the system is provided in Fig. 1 . While we acknowledge that handling the simultaneous presence of only 2 2 vehicles may appear as a limitation of our approach, the challenges that arise in multi-vehicle scenes are mainly related to the ability to detect and parse the presence of more than one simultaneous spectral signature. Our goal is to provide a proof-of-concept that it is possible to develop a multi-task pipeline able to handle planar localisation, classification and vehicle counting without relying on any sound-source separation method. Sound source separation, indeed, is pretty much still an open problem, especially in the wild [ 6 ] . Such a proof-of-concept can serve as a baseline for further approaches coping with several vehicles. Our methodological contribution is a two-stage pipeline: a self-supervised pre-training stage inspired by the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) [ 7 , 8 ] , applied directly to multichannel raw waveforms without spectral pre-processing, followed by supervised multi-task fine-tuning with a bidirectional LSTM and three classification heads. Rather than reconstructing raw audio, the encoder is trained to predict the latent representation of a future acoustic segment from its past context, thereby adopting a temporal prediction objective that encourages semantically meaningful structure and yields representations that are temporally stable and transferable across driving conditions. II Related Work Acoustic vehicle perception. Audio has been explored both as a complement to visual sensing and as an independent modality for early detection of traffic agents outside the field of view [ 9 , 10 ] . The first dataset explicitly designed to address NLOS scenarios was introduced in [ 1 ] , where the authors used SRP-PHAT [ 11 ] and a linear SVM to estimate the Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) of a vehicle, expressed as left, front, right, none . Subsequent work improved direction accuracy using CNN architectures [ 2 ] , jointly predicted the approach and departure directions [ 3 ] , and integrated acoustic cues with bird’s-eye-view spatial priors [ 4 ] . All these works perform only DoA estimation in single-vehicle scenarios. The DCASE community, through the Acoustic-Based Traffic Monitoring challenge and its baseline system [ 5 ] , investigated multi-vehicle localisation and classification relying on fixed roadside arrays. Yet, this setting does not fit the requirements of an autonomous vehicle’s planner: the sensors are stationary, rather than on-board, and estimates are provided every minute, making them very valuable for traffic monitoring, but not to trigger immediate interventions. Self-supervised audio representations. Contrastive methods [ 12 ] and masked reconstruction approaches [ 13 , 14 ] have shown that representations learned without labels on a large audio dataset can be reused across a broad range of downstream audio tasks. The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture [ 8 , 15 ] proposes a different objective: a predictor is trained to forecast the latent representation of a masked or future region from context, avoiding the cost of reconstructing perceptually irrelevant signal detail. Audio-JEPA [ 16 ] adapts this principle to mel-spectrogram patches and achieves competitive results on general audio benchmarks with large amounts of training data. We adapt the JEPA temporal prediction paradigm to operate directly on multichannel raw waveforms, letting the encoder free to learn from the raw signal whichever spectral, temporal, and cross-channel structure the prediction task actually rewards. Our contribution can be summarised as follows: 1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first on-board acoustic system that jointly estimates the direction , the number , and the class of multiple NLOS vehicles, with 1 1 -second latency. 2. We introduce a JEPA-inspired temporal-prediction objective trained directly on raw 8-channel waveforms, and show that it captures better representations than supervised models, which allows generalisation to unseen, and significantly different, scenarios. III Method We divide the description of the proposed framework into three parts: the temporal windowing of the input signal (Section III-A ), the self-supervised pre-training of the acoustic encoder (Section III-B ), and the supervised multi-task fine-tuning stage (Section III-C ). IV Experiments We run three main experiments: we evaluate the performance of our multi-task model and compare it with the state of the art ( Experiment 1 ); we carry out ablation studies to experimentally evaluate the rationale of our design choices ( Experiment 2 ); we investigate whether the model can generalise and robustly operate on unseen, and significantly different, scenarios ( Experiment 3 ). We indicate the three tasks: DoA estimation, vehicle type classification and number of vehicle estimation as Direction , Count and Type , respectively. Some qualitative results conclude the section. IV-A The Dataset To collect real‑world data, three MER2‑503‑36U3C cameras were mounted side‑by‑side on the roof of a vehicle, directly above an octagonal array of eight microphones. A GPS unit was also installed on the roof. An overview of the setup is shown in Fig. 3 . Each camera provides a 93 93 ° FoV at a resolution of 2448 × 2048 2448\times 2048 px at 20 20 fps, resulting in a combined horizontal coverage of approximately 279 279 °. Data collection took place at the SolarPark in Oldenburg, Germany. The dataset spans across 6 6 different scenarios ( cf. , Fig. 4 ), grouped into two main settings leading to two different datasets: the one we refer to as the T-Junction (TJ) one and the Take-Over (TO) one. In both cases, trials last between 10 10 and 30 30 s, depending on the vehicle’s speed and position. To reduce bias toward specific engine signatures, two different cars and two different vans were used. In the T-junction (TJ) dataset, the ego-vehicle is stationary at a T-junction. The dataset contains 6,827 6{,}827 labeled audio frames of 1 1 s: 1,958 1{,}958 with no vehicle present, 2,264 2{,}264 with a single vehicle approaching (left-to-right or right-to-left), and 2,605 2{,}605 with two vehicles approaching. In the Take Over (TO) dataset, the ego-vehicle is in motion, and one or two vehicles perform an overtake manoeuvre. The dataset contains 3,005 3{,}005 one-second labeled audio frames: 2,263 2{,}263 with one vehicle, and 742 742 with two. To annotate the dataset, when labels are not available directly from the experiments’ design, we leveraged the cameras and the labels given by YOLOv26x [ 19 ] running on the front camera images for static scenarios and on all three camera images for the others (mistakes were manually corrected). We assign labels for all the tasks we carry on: three classes ( 0 0 , 1 1 , 2 2 ) to indicate the numer of vehicles in the scene; four classes ( car, van, car+van, none ) to indicate the vehicle type, and five classes ( left, front, right, none, both ) to represent the direction of arrival/departure of a vehicle. More specifically, we assign the front label to any vehicle visible in the front camera’s 93 ∘ 93^{\circ} cone, left to vehicles entering or leaving via the left camera, and right via the right camera. The label both refers to two vehicles approaching from opposite directions, the label none indicates no vehicles. IV-B Experiment 1 Table I shows the performance of our model (indicated as Proposed ), and a comparison against the state of the art. We evaluate the accuracy in the Direction tasks of the models in [ 1 ] , [ 3 ] , and [ 2 ] , trained and tested on the TJ dataset (same split). Those models rely on a four-class schema for single-vehicle scenarios. Our method uses the extended five-class taxonomy, covering multiple simultaneous vehicles. Compared to the strongest prior result, even considering an additional class, our approach yields a 9.1 % 9.1\% improvement. We believe this is due to the JEPA-inspired stage of our method, capturing better representations compared to SOTA supervised models, and perform well also on smaller datasets, like ours. As being the only other work carrying out all three tasks, we also compare ourselves against [ 5 ] , trained and tested on the TJ dataset (same split). Our model shows an improvement of 21.2 % 21.2\% in the Direction task, 40.1 % 40.1\% in the Type task, and 5.6 % 5.6\% in the Count task. Table II (left columns) reports per-class recall on the TJ validation set. Classes none ( 94.4 % 94.4\% ) and both ( 100.0 % 100.0\% ) are the ones characterised by the highest accuracy: the absence of any acoustic source and the simultaneous presence of two vehicles coming from both sides produce discriminating signatures. The most often confused is the front class ( 60.0 % 60.0\% ), with the BiLSTM reacting with some delay to the class change. For instance, a vehicle approaching from the left, whose DoA is initially, and correctly, classified as left might be kept considered as such when it enters the front class. More details are provided in Section IV-E2 . Recall in the Count task exceeds 93 % 93\% across all classes, indicating that the self-supervised learning (SSL) representations encode the presence and number of distinct acoustic sources, without any architecture designed for counting. Vans achieve the highest recall ( 97.0 % 97.0\% ) in the Type task, likely due to their distinctive low-frequency engine signature. We can observe that the LSTM-only baseline provides the worst performance: without the SSL inductive bias, the supervised signal alone is insufficient to learn generalised representations. We also note that the difference between frozen and unfrozen learning at stage 2 does not impact performance much, but helps better appreciate the direction task. The Ablation - prediction-target compares three configurations of the same encoder-predictor architecture, differing only in which frames act as context and target. IV-E 2 Front-class error pathology In Experiment 1 the front class yield 60.0 % 60.0\% recall. In an attempt to investigate the reasons making it the hardest to recognise, we analyse when most errors take place. The intuition is that the Direction classes, identified by the cone described in Figure 3 are rather arbitrary and not acoustically grounded, thus mistakes in the transitions are physiological . We divide the class into three subclasses: entering, front, leaving . The entering subclass contains all samples corresponding to the first 1 1 s frame where the vehicle just becomes visible when entering the “front visible cone” from left or right. The leaving subclass contains all samples corresponding to the last 1 1 s frame where the vehicle is still visible before leaving from the “front visible cone” heading left or right. The front subclass contains all the remaining samples from the original front class. Fig. 5 reports the results of the analysis. As we can see, most mistakes happen when “transitioning” from the left / right classes to the front and viceversa, supporting the initial intuition. IV-E 3 Dynamics and Types Representations We analyse the SSL latent abilities to capture jointly the dynamics and the type of the sound sources, and ask what the representation actually contains without supervision. Figure 6 shows a UMAP [ 20 ] projection of the learned latents. Three structural facts are visible. First, silence consistently lives outside the active manifold: the none class of direction, the 0 class of count, and the none class of type occupy the same peripheral islands, indicating a stable no vehicle state separated from any vehicle activity. Second, the dominant axis within the active manifold separates one-vehicle from two-vehicle scenarios. Figure 6 -b shows a clean spatial gradient with two-vehicle frames ( 2 ) on the left and one-vehicle frames ( 1 ) on the right. Figure 6 -c inherits this structure since two-vehicle scenarios are always car+van pairs by recording protocol. Third, within the one-vehicle subset of 6 -c, car is less clustered than van , demonstrating a weaker representation of this class. Figure 6 -a shows that direction-of-arrival classes form recognisable regions: left (blue) and right (green) occupy opposite sides of the active manifold, both (orange) clusters tightly on the left edge where the two-vehicle region lies, and front (yellow) intermixes with the others, partially in coherence with the two opposite sides, but also highlighting the encoder’s limits to capture the spatial structure of that class. The framework works directly on the raw audio signals and provides robust predictions every second. Experimental evaluation showed that our method outperforms the state of the art, and further stressed the crucial role that auditory perception can play. Future work might proceed along two main directions: the extension to scenarios with more than 2 vehicles present, where localisation is refined to a regression task ( i.e. , from classes to continuous angles), and the integration into a multimodal system.
